Ciena’s Earnings Call Highlights AI-Fueled Growth Wave
Tipranks - Tipranks - Wed Sep 16, 7:06PM CDT
Ciena Corporation ((CIEN)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.
Ciena Corporation delivered a confident and upbeat earnings call, underscoring record revenue, margins, and EPS alongside surging orders and backlog. Management framed the quarter as evidence of a durable, AI-driven upcycle, while acknowledging supply constraints, higher near-term cash investments, and tariff uncertainties that may temper the pace, but not the trajectory, of growth.
Record Revenue and Profitability Break New Ground
Ciena posted Q3 revenue of $1.67 billion, a 37% year-on-year jump and another all-time quarterly high. Adjusted operating margin climbed to 22.5%, surpassing guidance and more than doubling versus last year, while adjusted EPS hit a record $2.11, up 215%, signaling powerful operating leverage.
Optical networks, including interconnects, grew more than 45% year on year, with RLS and WAV server systems each advancing over 55%. The in-and-around-the-data-center segment has already quadrupled year to date, outpacing Ciena’s promised 3x growth as direct cloud provider revenue leapt more than 80%.
Q3 book-to-bill was well above 1, driving backlog up by $800 million to $8.5 billion. Management expects backlog to exceed $10 billion by the end of fiscal 2026, and noted that just one month into Q4, orders booked were already approaching the full level of Q3.
Executives described an extraordinary AI-led demand backdrop for bandwidth and connectivity, with total addressable market seen doubling from roughly $25 billion to about $50 billion by 2029. Ciena expects not only a larger market but also a rising share of that expanding pie.
WaveLogic 6 Extreme Extends Technology Lead
WaveLogic 6 Extreme remains the only 1.6 terabit high-performance modem commercially available, 18 months after launch. Its ramp has already surpassed the prior-generation WaveLogic 5e, with growing adoption across both traditional wide-area networks and emerging AI WAN architectures.
RLS Strength and Hyper-Rail Build Momentum
Ciena’s RLS intelligent line systems hold an estimated 70% share and are viewed as the industry standard for disaggregated line systems. Orders for next-gen RLS Hyper-Rail are ramping, with initial customer standardization targeted by end-2026 and material revenue expected as scale builds from 2027 onward.
WaveLogic 5 nano pluggable optics continued to ramp, with Q3 shipments of 800ZR modules more than doubling quarter on quarter. The company highlighted strong interest in Nitro for active copper cables and early sample orders for Vesta, its open co-packaged optical solution aimed at next-generation data center architectures.
Ciena announced a notable hyperscaler victory, integrating WaveLogic 6 coherent technology directly into the customer’s own platform. The design combines Ciena’s DSPs, drivers, TIAs, and optical expertise into a full module slated for broad rollout across the client’s global optical footprint.
Adjusted gross margin reached 46.4%, up 450 basis points year on year and near the top of guidance even excluding a one-time tariff refund benefit. Management said disciplined costs, mix and pricing let them reset the margin baseline firmly in the mid-40s, with further expansion expected over the coming years.
Solid Free Cash Flow and Ample Liquidity
Despite higher working capital needs to support inventory and revenue growth, Ciena generated $116 million in free cash flow in Q3. The company ended the quarter with $2.8 billion in cash and equivalents, providing significant flexibility to invest in capacity, technology, and shareholder returns.
A June convertible offering gave Ciena a five-year zero-coupon instrument with a 114% economic conversion premium, enabling repayment of a 5.5% term loan. The company also repurchased 356,000 shares for $172 million in Q3, signaling confidence in long-term prospects and valuation.
Capital investments boosted capacity enough to support more than 60% year-to-date growth in RLS plug and WAV server revenue. Ciena has locked in long-term component agreements through 2029, is qualifying additional suppliers, and is exploring new technologies to strengthen supply resilience.
Customer discussions now include price increases from high single digits into the high teens or low twenties depending on product, with some hikes applied to backlog. Negotiations also encompass payment terms, fill rates, and mutual supply commitments, reflecting a broader value exchange rather than pure price hikes.
Around half of Ciena’s business now comes directly from hyperscalers, with neo-scalers expected to grow more important in 2027 and 2028. Demand spans RLS, Hyper-Rail, modems, MOFN, submarine networks and data center connectivity, with activity reported in India, the Middle East, North America and Asia.
Service Provider and Submarine Growth Tailwinds
Management sees steady service provider growth ahead, driven by years of underinvestment and renewed optical buildouts, including MOFN projects. Massive global submarine cable deployments, where Ciena claims the number-one market share, add another long-lived growth vector.
Scale-Across and Existing Data Center Focus
Scale-across connectivity between data centers was described as a major, still early-stage demand driver, particularly for North American hyperscalers. Much of the current visibility ties to existing facilities, GPU refresh cycles, capacity additions, inference traffic and network expansion rather than just new builds.
Software and Embedded Intelligence Still Matter
Web-scale deals tend to include fewer off-box software components, but Ciena stressed that customers still receive advanced on-box intelligence. These include protection mechanisms, planning and link-engineering tools, plus global service capabilities that underpin activation and service-level performance.
Attractive Economics for Hyper-Rail and Coherent
Management expects Hyper-Rail margins to be a step function above the already improved RLS profile, becoming accretive as volumes rise through 2027-2029. Ciena also sees coherent optics inside data centers as a major emerging market, with its planned 3.2-terabit solution positioned to capture early leadership.
Executives noted that fiscal 2027 revenue could exceed current guidance if more supply were available, but capacity remains limiting. The company cannot meet all backlog delivery requests for 2027 and expects the supply-demand imbalance to persist into 2028.
Ciena anticipates lower cash from operations in Q4, as it deploys capital to secure long-term supply agreements and upstream capacity. While this reduces near-term cash conversion, management views the spending as essential to support multiyear growth and customer commitments.
Working-Capital Cash Conversion Volatility
Quarterly working-capital cash conversion slipped versus the prior quarter, reflecting inventory and supply investments. However, executives said the broader trend versus year-ago levels remains positive, suggesting improving structural cash dynamics over time.
Tariff Refunds One-Off; Canadian Risk Monitored
The roughly 70-basis-point Q3 gross-margin boost from tariff refunds was a one-time accounting item that will not recur. Ciena is also assessing a new Canadian tariff regime that could carry a roughly $10 million quarterly impact and is pursuing mitigation strategies.
The R-S DCOM business is a net new addition that management describes as accretive to profitability. Still, revenue from this segment is expected to be lumpy quarter to quarter because of customer concentration and project timing.
Lower Off-Box Software in Web-Scale Deals
Management again acknowledged that web-scale contracts tend to include fewer separate software products than traditional deals. The company believes embedded software, tools and services still deliver substantial value and help support pricing and long-term relationships.
Ciena now expects fiscal 2026 operating expenses of about $1.6 billion, up from the earlier $1.5 billion view, including one-time variable compensation. Management plans to reinvest those amounts and further fund line systems and interconnect innovation to sustain competitiveness.
Guidance Signals Sustained Growth and Margin Strength
For Q4 fiscal 2026, Ciena guides revenue to about $1.75 billion, plus or minus $50 million, with adjusted gross margins near 45% and operating margin around 20%. For fiscal 2027, management projects revenue growth of at least 30% to $8.3-$8.4 billion, gross margin of 45-46%, operating margin of 25-27%, and a ramp of Hyper-Rail to several hundred million dollars.
Ciena’s earnings call painted a picture of a company riding powerful AI and optical networking tailwinds while carefully managing capacity, pricing and investment. Record financial results, rising backlog and strong technology positioning underpin a bullish long-term view, even as supply bottlenecks, tariffs and near-term cash outlays introduce some tactical challenges for investors to monitor.

Arista Networks Advances 4% While Ciena Soars 11% on AI Networking Demand; Cisco Rises 3%
Three networking and optical stocks are surging well past the broader market today, but the gaps between their gains reveal something specific about where AI infrastructure demand is hitting a wall.

Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.

AI networking demand is lifting Arista Networks (NYSE:ANET | ANET Price Prediction), Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) and Ciena (NYSE:CIEN), with shares of the optical supplier pulling far ahead of the two switching vendors. No company announcement accounts for the gain in Arista stock, which sits inside a broader bid across networking and optical equipment. That leaves the relative size of the three moves as the clearest signal of where the market sees demand outrunning supply.
Ciena stock is at $431.18, up 11% in midday trading, the largest gain of the three by a wide margin. Meanwhile, Arista Networks stock is at $214.34, up 4%, the smallest advance in the group. Cisco stock trades at $115.83, up 3%, landing between the other two.
For context, the iShares U.S. Technology ETF (NYSEARCA:IYW) is up 0.63%, a modest gain for the broader tech sector. At the same time, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 0.76%. Against those benchmarks, shares of Ciena, Arista and Cisco are each running well ahead of both the tech sector and the overall market, a sign that the buying is targeted at network equipment.
Bernstein Note Ties Networking to Optical
On October 1, Bernstein initiated coverage of Arista Networks with an Outperform rating and a price target of $250, arguing that networking and optical suppliers both benefit from AI infrastructure spending, with demand still running ahead of supply. That note is several days old and serves as background to the session. The detail that matters now is the note’s pairing of networking with optical, since shares of Ciena, the optical name in this group, are running hardest.
Arista Networks reported its second-quarter 2026 results in early August, with revenue growth of 37.7% from a year earlier. Demand across AI networking, data centers, campus and routing drove that growth, giving the company several engines working at once, and such breadth underpins Arista’s longer-term story, though the August report isn’t fresh news for the stock and doesn’t explain the latest buying on its own.
Transport Layer Shows Where Scarcity Sits
Inside data centers, Arista and Cisco sell the switches and routers that move traffic, while Ciena supplies the optical transport layer that carries traffic between those facilities. A buildout that adds computing capacity in more locations lifts transport demand before it lifts switching demand. That sequencing is the structural reason Ciena, Arista and Cisco shares don’t move in lockstep, even when the same AI theme is driving all three.
Ciena stock running several times harder than Arista stock points to the transport layer as the place where the market currently sees scarcity. Bernstein’s note collapsed exactly that distinction by grouping networking and optical suppliers together under one spending thesis. Arista stock is the smallest mover of the three, which complicates reading the session as a story about Arista itself.
Between those extremes, Cisco stock is advancing solidly, which suggests the bid extends across the equipment layer as a whole. The middle slot held by Cisco stock also gives the market a useful reference point, since a broad rally lifts the diversified networking giant while the sharpest gains collect in optical transport. Such a pattern fits a market rewarding AI infrastructure broadly. It reserves its biggest premium for the scarcest piece (we profiled seven of these non-chip AI suppliers, from networking to power and cooling, in a free report you can grab here).
Evidence that switching demand is tightening the way transport demand appears to be would tie the next move in Arista stock to the company specifically, and this session doesn’t supply it. Traders could look for signs that Arista faces the same supply pressure Bernstein described across networking and optical suppliers. Until then, Ciena stock remains a clearer expression of the transport scarcity the market is pricing.
Shareholders may want to keep an eye on whether Cisco stock continues advancing alongside Ciena and Arista, since a sustained broad rally would support the view that AI networking spending is lifting every tier of the equipment stack. A fade in CSCO stock while CIEN stock holds its gains would point to a narrower trade concentrated in optical transport. Either outcome may clarify whether the equipment rally has staying power beyond the optical names.
Ciena stock carries the most risk of the three if transport scarcity eases, since it is running so far ahead of the group, while Arista and Cisco shares are riding the same spending wave with smaller swings. Investors weighing their exposure should calibrate their holdings carefully given that a sector-wide bid across networking and optical equipment is driving all three stocks. Keeping their positions in any one of these names moderate limits how much their portfolios lean on a single tier of the AI networking buildout.

Ciena Fell 40%—Now One Analyst Sees 50% Upside
Ciena Corp.
Interested in Ciena Corporation? Here are five stocks we like better.
Evercore ISI analyst Amit Daryanani upgraded Ciena to Outperform with a $550 price target, citing optical networking as an overlooked AI infrastructure bottleneck.
Ciena's stock fell more than 40% from its June high but has climbed about 17% in less than three weeks amid renewed investor interest.
Ciena posted 37% year-over-year revenue growth and 215% EPS growth, with a backlog expected to exceed $10 billion by fiscal year-end.
Despite all the money pouring into the artificial intelligence boom, it feels like only a small handful of names have been consistent winners.
Plenty of companies quietly making that boom possible have been overlooked, their shares languishing while the giants soar. Ciena Corporation (NYSE: CIEN) is a good example.
Despite sitting right in the path of the AI wave, its stock has nonetheless tumbled more than 40% from its June high. However, that disconnect may be correcting itself.
After a punishing slide, the stock appears to have found a floor early this month and has started to turn higher, climbing around 17% in less than three weeks.
Even after its fall, Ciena is still up roughly 50% for the year, and the current bounce suggests investors are beginning to look again at a name they had written off. A well-timed vote of confidence from Wall Street this week has helped, making this a perfect time to ask if the market has been way too negative on Ciena’s prospects.
That vote of confidence came from Evercore ISI, with analyst Amit Daryanani upgrading Ciena to Outperform earlier this week and setting a $550 price target. From where the stock trades today, that's around 50% upside, and just as importantly, Daryanani's argument cuts to the heart of the bull case: that Ciena sits at one of the AI boom's most overlooked bottlenecks.
This bottleneck theory is simple. Amid all the noise about chips and computing power, far less attention goes to how that data actually moves around. Modern AI systems shuttle staggering volumes of information between and within data centers, and doing so fast enough has become a serious constraint on how powerful they can be. Daryanani pinpointed connectivity as an increasingly critical bottleneck to the pace of AI's advancement.
This is Ciena's world. The company specializes in optical networking, the high-speed connections that carry data over long distances and, increasingly, across the sprawling AI facilities springing up everywhere. As one of the few dedicated names in the field, it’s particularly well placed to benefit as those systems, and their data demands, keep growing.
The bullish case is more than a story, because the numbers behind it are seriously impressive. In its most recent quarterly report, released earlier this month, Ciena reported year-on-year revenue growth of 37% and earnings per share growth of 215%.
More telling still is the pipeline of future work. Ciena’s management pointed to a swelling order book, with its backlog expected to top $10 billion by the end of its financial year, giving it, and the market, solid visibility into future revenue.
Ciena is also pushing into new territory. Beyond its traditional strength in long-distance links, it's developing products that operate inside data centers themselves, chasing a market it believes could be worth many billions. With leading technology and a clutch of new products, it has several ways to win rather than relying on a single one.
None of this means the risks have vanished. The stock's steep fall from its June high and the volatility that followed remind us how quickly sentiment can turn on a name like this. The biggest worry is simply that the AI spending spree may not last, and Ciena's fortunes are tightly bound to how much the cloud giants keep investing, so any slowdown would hit its orders hard.
There’s also the matter of who its customers are. A handful of large clients account for a hefty slice of Ciena's revenue, with one customer alone making up close to 20%. Such concentration cuts both ways: it’s fine while those customers spend freely, but it would hurt if even one pulled back.
Weighing it up, Ciena makes a compelling case as an underappreciated way to play the AI infrastructure boom. It sits at a real bottleneck, its core business is growing fast, its order book offers rare visibility, and Wall Street is clearly leaning toward the upside.
The caution comes not from the bulls but from the setup itself. Ciena's shares remain volatile, its valuation demands strong growth for years to come, and expectations will likely stay high after this week's upgrade. That tension, between an early-stage turnaround and a business with a lot still to prove, is what keeps the stock finely balanced.
For those who believe the AI buildout has years left to run, though, Ciena increasingly looks like one of its more overlooked beneficiaries, and this week's upgrade is a clear sign that others are already catching on.

The combination of AI-driven data traffic, hyperscaler infrastructure spending, and the transition toward higher-speed optical connectivity could provide Ciena with a significant growth runway.

Here's What You May Not Know About Analysts' Price Targets
According to researchers at several universities across the globe, a price target is one of many pieces of information about a stock that misleads investors far more often than it guides. In fact, empirical research shows that price targets set by several analysts, irrespective of the extent of agreement, rarely indicate where the price of a stock could actually be heading.
While Wall Street analysts have deep knowledge of a company's fundamentals and the sensitivity of its business to economic and industry issues, many of them tend to set overly optimistic price targets. Are you wondering why?
They usually do that to drum up interest in shares of companies that their firms either have existing business relationships with or are looking to be associated with. In other words, business incentives of firms covering a stock often result in inflated price targets set by analysts.
However, a tight clustering of price targets, which is represented by a low standard deviation, indicates that analysts have a high degree of agreement about the direction and magnitude of a stock's price movement. While that doesn't necessarily mean the stock will hit the average price target, it could be a good starting point for further research aimed at identifying the potential fundamental driving forces.
That said, while investors should not entirely ignore price targets, making an investment decision solely based on them could lead to disappointing ROI. So, price targets should always be treated with a high degree of skepticism.
There has been increasing optimism among analysts lately about the company's earnings prospects, as indicated by strong agreement among them in revising EPS estimates higher. Evercore and Bernstein Make the Optical Case
Evercore ISI analyst Amit Daryanani upgraded Ciena stock to Outperform late last week and raised the firm’s price target to $550. Daryanani’s argument is that an AI system runs only as fast as the chips inside it can exchange information across server racks and between data centers. When those connections fall behind, operators lose efficiency. They struggle to get full use of equipment they’ve already paid for, and Daryanani sees the opportunity in Ciena’s optical networking technology, which moves that traffic inside data centers and over longer distances.
Bernstein added to the momentum in the previous session, launching coverage of Ciena stock at Outperform as part of a positive rollout across the U.S. networking group. In that research, Bernstein told investors that networking and optical companies stand to be structural winners within AI infrastructure. Both calls point at the same bottleneck, and Ciena sells the optical transport that lets data centers, and the links between them, keep pace with the compute being installed around them.
Ciena’s Own Re-Rating Stands Apart From Its Peers
Ciena stock is up 59% year to date, so the two analyst calls are landing on a name that has already run a long way. Evercore ISI’s higher price target arriving after that kind of climb raises the bar into strength, at a point when the market was already rewarding Ciena’s optical franchise.
Arista and Cisco shares are barely moving alongside Ciena stock, suggesting the market views the analyst calls as specific to Ciena. Extreme Networks (NASDAQ:EXTR), a smaller enterprise networking peer, rounds out the group.

Much of that story may already be priced in after this year’s run, so any slowdown in AI infrastructure spending could weigh on the shares.

Anyone sizing up their exposure should adjust their holdings carefully given that Ciena stock is up 59% year to date and the latest price target raise arrived into strength. Keeping one’s Ciena stake moderate leaves room to benefit from the AI networking demand case both firms laid out while limiting the damage if momentum in CIEN stock fades.

Ciena's Optical Tech Gets a Boost From CtrlS Deployment
As AI, cloud computing and hyperscale infrastructure expand, the ability to move enormous volumes of data quickly between facilities is becoming exceedingly important. Against this backdrop, CtrlS Datacenters is working with Ciena Corporation CIEN to build five metro networks connecting nine data centers across Chennai, Hyderabad, Kolkata, New Delhi and Noida in India, with the networks designed to deliver up to 100 Tb/s of capacity. The deployment is part of a larger Managed Optical Fiber Network (MOFN) project for a leading hyperscaler.
Ciena highlights metro data center interconnect as a way to provide high-capacity, resilient connectivity between metro data centers, an architecture increasingly relevant as cloud and AI infrastructure becomes more distributed. Ciena has identified MOFN as a growing opportunity associated with distributed AI infrastructure. In its recent research, 96% of surveyed service providers expected MOFN services to generate revenue from connecting distributed AI compute clusters over the next three years.
CtrlS is deploying Ciena's WaveLogic 5 Extreme (WL5e)-powered Waveserver platform alongside the 6500 Reconfigurable Line System (RLS). The Waveserver platform is designed for high-capacity optical connectivity, while the 6500 RLS provides the optical transport infrastructure needed to scale network capacity. Ciena's broader technology roadmap reflects the direction of the optical industry. The company recently highlighted 1.6 Tb/s coherent optical capabilities and other technologies designed to support AI-scale networking. Although this CtrlS deployment uses WL5e, the broader evolution of Ciena's coherent optics portfolio illustrates the industry's move toward increasingly high-capacity optical transport.
The project also fits Ciena's broader strategy around AI-driven network investment. Recently, it was selected by the Africa Coast to Europe cable system consortium to upgrade a roughly 17,000-km route connecting Western Europe, West Africa and South Africa. Additionally, FLAG deployed Ciena's WL6e technology on its dedicated fiber pair in the ECHO trans-Pacific subsea cable system connecting Singapore, Guam and California. Ciena reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $1.67 billion, up 37% year over year, and raised its fiscal 2026 revenue guidance to approximately $6.42 billion at the midpoint. The company has repeatedly pointed to AI-related connectivity demand, hyperscaler infrastructure and MOFN as structural drivers for its business.
How Does CIEN Stack Up in the Optical Networking Market?
Corning Incorporated GLW entered the second half of 2026 with its growth outlook tied to AI infrastructure and optical connectivity. Corning is also expanding its GenAI optical portfolio with multicore fiber and high-density connectivity solutions that improve network capacity and reduce installation complexity. It announced a long-term partnership with NVIDIA to expand U.S.-based optical connectivity manufacturing capacity by 10 times and increase domestic fiber production capacity by more than 50%. In September, Corning secured a multiyear, multibillion-dollar Verizon deal to supply more than 80 million miles of optical fiber through 2032, boosting revenue visibility and exposure to broadband and AI infrastructure demand.
Nokia NOK continues to benefit from its broad portfolio spanning mobile networks, optical transport, IP routing, fixed broadband, software and services. Network Infrastructure delivered double-digit growth in second-quarter 2026, supported by continued momentum in Optical Networks and IP Networks. The planned divestiture of the Fixed Wireless Access CPE business simplifies the portfolio and allows greater investment in higher-growth opportunities such as AI networking and optical technologies. NOK is also expanding U.S. optical manufacturing capacity through investments in San Jose, PA and the planned acquisition of an additional semiconductor manufacturing site in Arizona. Management noted that supply constraints persist in optical networking, supporting longer-term customer orders.

Shares of CIEN have gained 147.6% in the past year compared with the Communications - Components industry's surge of 140.5%.
CIEN trades at a forward 12-month price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 35.72, above the industry's 35.31.

Ciena Fell 40%—Now One Analyst Sees 50% Upside
Ciena logo on a red wall in a data center corridor with illuminated fiber optic cables and server racks.
Interested in Ciena Corporation? Here are five stocks we like better.
Evercore ISI analyst Amit Daryanani upgraded Ciena to Outperform with a $550 price target, citing optical networking as an overlooked AI infrastructure bottleneck.
Ciena's stock fell more than 40% from its June high but has climbed about 17% in less than three weeks amid renewed investor interest.
Ciena posted 37% year-over-year revenue growth and 215% EPS growth, with a backlog expected to exceed $10 billion by fiscal year-end.
Despite all the money pouring into the artificial intelligence boom, it feels like only a small handful of names have been consistent winners.
Plenty of companies quietly making that boom possible have been overlooked, their shares languishing while the giants soar. Ciena Corporation (NYSE: CIEN) is a good example.
→ Sandisk Joins the S&P 100—Is the Index Flow, or the AI Story, Driving the Stock?
Despite sitting right in the path of the AI wave, its stock has nonetheless tumbled more than 40% from its June high. However, that disconnect may be correcting itself.
After a punishing slide, the stock appears to have found a floor early this month and has started to turn higher, climbing around 17% in less than three weeks.
→ Viking's Obesity Edge May Be Staying Power, Not Weight Loss
Even after its fall, Ciena is still up roughly 50% for the year, and the current bounce suggests investors are beginning to look again at a name they had written off. A well-timed vote of confidence from Wall Street this week has helped, making this a perfect time to ask if the market has been way too negative on Ciena's prospects.
That vote of confidence came from Evercore ISI, with analyst Amit Daryanani upgrading Ciena to Outperform earlier this week and setting a $550 price target. From where the stock trades today, that's around 50% upside, and just as importantly, Daryanani's argument cuts to the heart of the bull case: that Ciena sits at one of the AI boom's most overlooked bottlenecks.
→ Full Throttle: Kratos and GE Fire Up a Next-Gen Defense Engine
This bottleneck theory is simple. Amid all the noise about chips and computing power, far less attention goes to how that data actually moves around. Modern AI systems shuttle staggering volumes of information between and within data centers, and doing so fast enough has become a serious constraint on how powerful they can be. Daryanani pinpointed connectivity as an increasingly critical bottleneck to the pace of AI's advancement.
This is Ciena's world. The company specializes in optical networking, the high-speed connections that carry data over long distances and, increasingly, across the sprawling AI facilities springing up everywhere. As one of the few dedicated names in the field, it's particularly well placed to benefit as those systems, and their data demands, keep growing.
The bullish case is more than a story, because the numbers behind it are seriously impressive. In its most recent quarterly report, released earlier this month, Ciena reported year-on-year revenue growth of 37% and earnings per share growth of 215%.
More telling still is the pipeline of future work. Ciena's management pointed to a swelling order book, with its backlog expected to top $10 billion by the end of its financial year, giving it, and the market, solid visibility into future revenue.
Ciena is also pushing into new territory. Beyond its traditional strength in long-distance links, it's developing products that operate inside data centers themselves, chasing a market it believes could be worth many billions. With leading technology and a clutch of new products, it has several ways to win rather than relying on a single one.
None of this means the risks have vanished. The stock's steep fall from its June high and the volatility that followed remind us how quickly sentiment can turn on a name like this. The biggest worry is simply that the AI spending spree may not last, and Ciena's fortunes are tightly bound to how much the cloud giants keep investing, so any slowdown would hit its orders hard.
There's also the matter of who its customers are. A handful of large clients account for a hefty slice of Ciena's revenue, with one customer alone making up close to 20%. Such concentration cuts both ways: it's fine while those customers spend freely, but it would hurt if even one pulled back.
Weighing it up, Ciena makes a compelling case as an underappreciated way to play the AI infrastructure boom. It sits at a real bottleneck, its core business is growing fast, its order book offers rare visibility, and Wall Street is clearly leaning toward the upside.
The caution comes not from the bulls but from the setup itself. Ciena's shares remain volatile, its valuation demands strong growth for years to come, and expectations will likely stay high after this week's upgrade. That tension, between an early-stage turnaround and a business with a lot still to prove, is what keeps the stock finely balanced.
For those who believe the AI buildout has years left to run, though, Ciena increasingly looks like one of its more overlooked beneficiaries, and this week's upgrade is a clear sign that others are already catching on.

Ciena’s Earnings Call Highlights AI-Fueled Growth Wave
Tipranks - Tipranks - Wed Sep 16, 7:06PM CDT
Ciena Corporation ((CIEN)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.
Ciena Corporation delivered a confident and upbeat earnings call, underscoring record revenue, margins, and EPS alongside surging orders and backlog. Management framed the quarter as evidence of a durable, AI-driven upcycle, while acknowledging supply constraints, higher near-term cash investments, and tariff uncertainties that may temper the pace, but not the trajectory, of growth.
Record Revenue and Profitability Break New Ground
Ciena posted Q3 revenue of $1.67 billion, a 37% year-on-year jump and another all-time quarterly high. Adjusted operating margin climbed to 22.5%, surpassing guidance and more than doubling versus last year, while adjusted EPS hit a record $2.11, up 215%, signaling powerful operating leverage.
Optical networks, including interconnects, grew more than 45% year on year, with RLS and WAV server systems each advancing over 55%. The in-and-around-the-data-center segment has already quadrupled year to date, outpacing Ciena’s promised 3x growth as direct cloud provider revenue leapt more than 80%.
Q3 book-to-bill was well above 1, driving backlog up by $800 million to $8.5 billion. Management expects backlog to exceed $10 billion by the end of fiscal 2026, and noted that just one month into Q4, orders booked were already approaching the full level of Q3.
Executives described an extraordinary AI-led demand backdrop for bandwidth and connectivity, with total addressable market seen doubling from roughly $25 billion to about $50 billion by 2029. Ciena expects not only a larger market but also a rising share of that expanding pie.
WaveLogic 6 Extreme Extends Technology Lead
WaveLogic 6 Extreme remains the only 1.6 terabit high-performance modem commercially available, 18 months after launch. Its ramp has already surpassed the prior-generation WaveLogic 5e, with growing adoption across both traditional wide-area networks and emerging AI WAN architectures.
RLS Strength and Hyper-Rail Build Momentum
Ciena’s RLS intelligent line systems hold an estimated 70% share and are viewed as the industry standard for disaggregated line systems. Orders for next-gen RLS Hyper-Rail are ramping, with initial customer standardization targeted by end-2026 and material revenue expected as scale builds from 2027 onward.
WaveLogic 5 nano pluggable optics continued to ramp, with Q3 shipments of 800ZR modules more than doubling quarter on quarter. The company highlighted strong interest in Nitro for active copper cables and early sample orders for Vesta, its open co-packaged optical solution aimed at next-generation data center architectures.
Ciena announced a notable hyperscaler victory, integrating WaveLogic 6 coherent technology directly into the customer’s own platform. The design combines Ciena’s DSPs, drivers, TIAs, and optical expertise into a full module slated for broad rollout across the client’s global optical footprint.
Adjusted gross margin reached 46.4%, up 450 basis points year on year and near the top of guidance even excluding a one-time tariff refund benefit. Management said disciplined costs, mix and pricing let them reset the margin baseline firmly in the mid-40s, with further expansion expected over the coming years.
Solid Free Cash Flow and Ample Liquidity
Despite higher working capital needs to support inventory and revenue growth, Ciena generated $116 million in free cash flow in Q3. The company ended the quarter with $2.8 billion in cash and equivalents, providing significant flexibility to invest in capacity, technology, and shareholder returns.
A June convertible offering gave Ciena a five-year zero-coupon instrument with a 114% economic conversion premium, enabling repayment of a 5.5% term loan. The company also repurchased 356,000 shares for $172 million in Q3, signaling confidence in long-term prospects and valuation.
Capital investments boosted capacity enough to support more than 60% year-to-date growth in RLS plug and WAV server revenue. Ciena has locked in long-term component agreements through 2029, is qualifying additional suppliers, and is exploring new technologies to strengthen supply resilience.
Customer discussions now include price increases from high single digits into the high teens or low twenties depending on product, with some hikes applied to backlog. Negotiations also encompass payment terms, fill rates, and mutual supply commitments, reflecting a broader value exchange rather than pure price hikes.
Around half of Ciena’s business now comes directly from hyperscalers, with neo-scalers expected to grow more important in 2027 and 2028. Demand spans RLS, Hyper-Rail, modems, MOFN, submarine networks and data center connectivity, with activity reported in India, the Middle East, North America and Asia.
Service Provider and Submarine Growth Tailwinds
Management sees steady service provider growth ahead, driven by years of underinvestment and renewed optical buildouts, including MOFN projects. Massive global submarine cable deployments, where Ciena claims the number-one market share, add another long-lived growth vector.
Scale-Across and Existing Data Center Focus
Scale-across connectivity between data centers was described as a major, still early-stage demand driver, particularly for North American hyperscalers. Much of the current visibility ties to existing facilities, GPU refresh cycles, capacity additions, inference traffic and network expansion rather than just new builds.
Software and Embedded Intelligence Still Matter
Web-scale deals tend to include fewer off-box software components, but Ciena stressed that customers still receive advanced on-box intelligence. These include protection mechanisms, planning and link-engineering tools, plus global service capabilities that underpin activation and service-level performance.
Attractive Economics for Hyper-Rail and Coherent
Management expects Hyper-Rail margins to be a step function above the already improved RLS profile, becoming accretive as volumes rise through 2027-2029. Ciena also sees coherent optics inside data centers as a major emerging market, with its planned 3.2-terabit solution positioned to capture early leadership.
Executives noted that fiscal 2027 revenue could exceed current guidance if more supply were available, but capacity remains limiting. The company cannot meet all backlog delivery requests for 2027 and expects the supply-demand imbalance to persist into 2028.
Ciena anticipates lower cash from operations in Q4, as it deploys capital to secure long-term supply agreements and upstream capacity. While this reduces near-term cash conversion, management views the spending as essential to support multiyear growth and customer commitments.
Working-Capital Cash Conversion Volatility
Quarterly working-capital cash conversion slipped versus the prior quarter, reflecting inventory and supply investments. However, executives said the broader trend versus year-ago levels remains positive, suggesting improving structural cash dynamics over time.
Tariff Refunds One-Off; Canadian Risk Monitored
The roughly 70-basis-point Q3 gross-margin boost from tariff refunds was a one-time accounting item that will not recur. Ciena is also assessing a new Canadian tariff regime that could carry a roughly $10 million quarterly impact and is pursuing mitigation strategies.
The R-S DCOM business is a net new addition that management describes as accretive to profitability. Still, revenue from this segment is expected to be lumpy quarter to quarter because of customer concentration and project timing.
Lower Off-Box Software in Web-Scale Deals
Management again acknowledged that web-scale contracts tend to include fewer separate software products than traditional deals. The company believes embedded software, tools and services still deliver substantial value and help support pricing and long-term relationships.
Ciena now expects fiscal 2026 operating expenses of about $1.6 billion, up from the earlier $1.5 billion view, including one-time variable compensation. Management plans to reinvest those amounts and further fund line systems and interconnect innovation to sustain competitiveness.
Guidance Signals Sustained Growth and Margin Strength
For Q4 fiscal 2026, Ciena guides revenue to about $1.75 billion, plus or minus $50 million, with adjusted gross margins near 45% and operating margin around 20%. For fiscal 2027, management projects revenue growth of at least 30% to $8.3-$8.4 billion, gross margin of 45-46%, operating margin of 25-27%, and a ramp of Hyper-Rail to several hundred million dollars.
Ciena’s earnings call painted a picture of a company riding powerful AI and optical networking tailwinds while carefully managing capacity, pricing and investment. Record financial results, rising backlog and strong technology positioning underpin a bullish long-term view, even as supply bottlenecks, tariffs and near-term cash outlays introduce some tactical challenges for investors to monitor.

AI networking demand is lifting Arista Networks (NYSE:ANET | ANET Price Prediction), Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) and Ciena (NYSE:CIEN), with shares of the optical supplier pulling far ahead of the two switching vendors. No company announcement accounts for the gain in Arista stock, which sits inside a broader bid across networking and optical equipment. That leaves the relative size of the three moves as the clearest signal of where the market sees demand outrunning supply.
Ciena stock is at $431.18, up 11% in midday trading, the largest gain of the three by a wide margin. Meanwhile, Arista Networks stock is at $214.34, up 4%, the smallest advance in the group. Cisco stock trades at $115.83, up 3%, landing between the other two.
For context, the iShares U.S. Technology ETF (NYSEARCA:IYW) is up 0.63%, a modest gain for the broader tech sector. At the same time, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 0.76%. Against those benchmarks, shares of Ciena, Arista and Cisco are each running well ahead of both the tech sector and the overall market, a sign that the buying is targeted at network equipment.
Bernstein Note Ties Networking to Optical
On October 1, Bernstein initiated coverage of Arista Networks with an Outperform rating and a price target of $250, arguing that networking and optical suppliers both benefit from AI infrastructure spending, with demand still running ahead of supply. That note is several days old and serves as background to the session. The detail that matters now is the note’s pairing of networking with optical, since shares of Ciena, the optical name in this group, are running hardest.
Arista Networks reported its second-quarter 2026 results in early August, with revenue growth of 37.7% from a year earlier. Demand across AI networking, data centers, campus and routing drove that growth, giving the company several engines working at once, and such breadth underpins Arista’s longer-term story, though the August report isn’t fresh news for the stock and doesn’t explain the latest buying on its own.
Transport Layer Shows Where Scarcity Sits
Inside data centers, Arista and Cisco sell the switches and routers that move traffic, while Ciena supplies the optical transport layer that carries traffic between those facilities. A buildout that adds computing capacity in more locations lifts transport demand before it lifts switching demand. That sequencing is the structural reason Ciena, Arista and Cisco shares don’t move in lockstep, even when the same AI theme is driving all three.
Ciena stock running several times harder than Arista stock points to the transport layer as the place where the market currently sees scarcity. Bernstein’s note collapsed exactly that distinction by grouping networking and optical suppliers together under one spending thesis. Arista stock is the smallest mover of the three, which complicates reading the session as a story about Arista itself.
Between those extremes, Cisco stock is advancing solidly, which suggests the bid extends across the equipment layer as a whole. The middle slot held by Cisco stock also gives the market a useful reference point, since a broad rally lifts the diversified networking giant while the sharpest gains collect in optical transport. Such a pattern fits a market rewarding AI infrastructure broadly. It reserves its biggest premium for the scarcest piece (we profiled seven of these non-chip AI suppliers, from networking to power and cooling, in a free report you can grab here).
Evidence that switching demand is tightening the way transport demand appears to be would tie the next move in Arista stock to the company specifically, and this session doesn’t supply it. Traders could look for signs that Arista faces the same supply pressure Bernstein described across networking and optical suppliers. Until then, Ciena stock remains a clearer expression of the transport scarcity the market is pricing.
Shareholders may want to keep an eye on whether Cisco stock continues advancing alongside Ciena and Arista, since a sustained broad rally would support the view that AI networking spending is lifting every tier of the equipment stack. A fade in CSCO stock while CIEN stock holds its gains would point to a narrower trade concentrated in optical transport. Either outcome may clarify whether the equipment rally has staying power beyond the optical names.
Ciena stock carries the most risk of the three if transport scarcity eases, since it is running so far ahead of the group, while Arista and Cisco shares are riding the same spending wave with smaller swings. Investors weighing their exposure should calibrate their holdings carefully given that a sector-wide bid across networking and optical equipment is driving all three stocks. Keeping their positions in any one of these names moderate limits how much their portfolios lean on a single tier of the AI networking buildout.

Despite all the money pouring into the artificial intelligence boom, it feels like only a small handful of names have been consistent winners.
Plenty of companies quietly making that boom possible have been overlooked, their shares languishing while the giants soar. Ciena Corporation (NYSE: CIEN) is a good example.
Despite sitting right in the path of the AI wave, its stock has nonetheless tumbled more than 40% from its June high. However, that disconnect may be correcting itself.
After a punishing slide, the stock appears to have found a floor early this month and has started to turn higher, climbing around 17% in less than three weeks.
Even after its fall, Ciena is still up roughly 50% for the year, and the current bounce suggests investors are beginning to look again at a name they had written off. A well-timed vote of confidence from Wall Street this week has helped, making this a perfect time to ask if the market has been way too negative on Ciena’s prospects.
That vote of confidence came from Evercore ISI, with analyst Amit Daryanani upgrading Ciena to Outperform earlier this week and setting a $550 price target. From where the stock trades today, that's around 50% upside, and just as importantly, Daryanani's argument cuts to the heart of the bull case: that Ciena sits at one of the AI boom's most overlooked bottlenecks.
This bottleneck theory is simple. Amid all the noise about chips and computing power, far less attention goes to how that data actually moves around. Modern AI systems shuttle staggering volumes of information between and within data centers, and doing so fast enough has become a serious constraint on how powerful they can be. Daryanani pinpointed connectivity as an increasingly critical bottleneck to the pace of AI's advancement.
This is Ciena's world. The company specializes in optical networking, the high-speed connections that carry data over long distances and, increasingly, across the sprawling AI facilities springing up everywhere. As one of the few dedicated names in the field, it’s particularly well placed to benefit as those systems, and their data demands, keep growing.
The bullish case is more than a story, because the numbers behind it are seriously impressive. In its most recent quarterly report, released earlier this month, Ciena reported year-on-year revenue growth of 37% and earnings per share growth of 215%.
More telling still is the pipeline of future work. Ciena’s management pointed to a swelling order book, with its backlog expected to top $10 billion by the end of its financial year, giving it, and the market, solid visibility into future revenue.
Ciena is also pushing into new territory. Beyond its traditional strength in long-distance links, it's developing products that operate inside data centers themselves, chasing a market it believes could be worth many billions. With leading technology and a clutch of new products, it has several ways to win rather than relying on a single one.
None of this means the risks have vanished. The stock's steep fall from its June high and the volatility that followed remind us how quickly sentiment can turn on a name like this. The biggest worry is simply that the AI spending spree may not last, and Ciena's fortunes are tightly bound to how much the cloud giants keep investing, so any slowdown would hit its orders hard.
There’s also the matter of who its customers are. A handful of large clients account for a hefty slice of Ciena's revenue, with one customer alone making up close to 20%. Such concentration cuts both ways: it’s fine while those customers spend freely, but it would hurt if even one pulled back.
Weighing it up, Ciena makes a compelling case as an underappreciated way to play the AI infrastructure boom. It sits at a real bottleneck, its core business is growing fast, its order book offers rare visibility, and Wall Street is clearly leaning toward the upside.
The caution comes not from the bulls but from the setup itself. Ciena's shares remain volatile, its valuation demands strong growth for years to come, and expectations will likely stay high after this week's upgrade. That tension, between an early-stage turnaround and a business with a lot still to prove, is what keeps the stock finely balanced.
For those who believe the AI buildout has years left to run, though, Ciena increasingly looks like one of its more overlooked beneficiaries, and this week's upgrade is a clear sign that others are already catching on.

Here's What You May Not Know About Analysts' Price Targets
According to researchers at several universities across the globe, a price target is one of many pieces of information about a stock that misleads investors far more often than it guides. In fact, empirical research shows that price targets set by several analysts, irrespective of the extent of agreement, rarely indicate where the price of a stock could actually be heading.
While Wall Street analysts have deep knowledge of a company's fundamentals and the sensitivity of its business to economic and industry issues, many of them tend to set overly optimistic price targets. Are you wondering why?
They usually do that to drum up interest in shares of companies that their firms either have existing business relationships with or are looking to be associated with. In other words, business incentives of firms covering a stock often result in inflated price targets set by analysts.
However, a tight clustering of price targets, which is represented by a low standard deviation, indicates that analysts have a high degree of agreement about the direction and magnitude of a stock's price movement. While that doesn't necessarily mean the stock will hit the average price target, it could be a good starting point for further research aimed at identifying the potential fundamental driving forces.
That said, while investors should not entirely ignore price targets, making an investment decision solely based on them could lead to disappointing ROI. So, price targets should always be treated with a high degree of skepticism.

A week of upbeat sell-side research on artificial intelligence (AI) networking is showing up in shares of Ciena (NYSE:CIEN | CIEN Price Prediction). Ciena stock is at $371.68, up 6% in early trading action. With the company itself quiet on news, the gain looks like the market catching up to a sell-side re-rating of Ciena stock that’s been building for a week.
Meanwhile, shares of fellow AI networking supplier Arista Networks (NYSE:ANET) are at $205.30, up 0.8%. Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) stock is holding steady at $107.94, up 0.3%. That split leaves Ciena stock out in front of the networking group by a wide margin.

Evercore and Bernstein Make the Optical Case
Evercore ISI analyst Amit Daryanani upgraded Ciena stock to Outperform late last week and raised the firm’s price target to $550. Daryanani’s argument is that an AI system runs only as fast as the chips inside it can exchange information across server racks and between data centers. When those connections fall behind, operators lose efficiency. They struggle to get full use of equipment they’ve already paid for, and Daryanani sees the opportunity in Ciena’s optical networking technology, which moves that traffic inside data centers and over longer distances.
Bernstein added to the momentum in the previous session, launching coverage of Ciena stock at Outperform as part of a positive rollout across the U.S. networking group. In that research, Bernstein told investors that networking and optical companies stand to be structural winners within AI infrastructure. Both calls point at the same bottleneck, and Ciena sells the optical transport that lets data centers, and the links between them, keep pace with the compute being installed around them.
Ciena’s Own Re-Rating Stands Apart From Its Peers
Ciena stock is up 59% year to date, so the two analyst calls are landing on a name that has already run a long way. Evercore ISI’s higher price target arriving after that kind of climb raises the bar into strength, at a point when the market was already rewarding Ciena’s optical franchise.
Arista and Cisco shares are barely moving alongside Ciena stock, suggesting the market views the analyst calls as specific to Ciena. Extreme Networks (NASDAQ:EXTR), a smaller enterprise networking peer, rounds out the group.
Both firms point to a bottleneck supporting the bullish thesis, where every new rack of AI chips depends on faster optical links (we highlighted seven suppliers solving exactly these AI expansion bottlenecks, from power to networking, in a free report here). Much of that story may already be priced in after this year’s run, so any slowdown in AI infrastructure spending could weigh on the shares.
It’s worth watching whether other firms follow Evercore ISI and Bernstein with bullish research on Ciena. Any pickup in Arista or Cisco shares toward Ciena’s pace could signal the buying is spreading across AI networking.
Anyone sizing up their exposure should adjust their holdings carefully given that Ciena stock is up 59% year to date and the latest price target raise arrived into strength. Keeping one’s Ciena stake moderate leaves room to benefit from the AI networking demand case both firms laid out while limiting the damage if momentum in CIEN stock fades.

As AI, cloud computing and hyperscale infrastructure expand, the ability to move enormous volumes of data quickly between facilities is becoming exceedingly important. Ciena has identified MOFN as a growing opportunity associated with distributed AI infrastructure. In its recent research, 96% of surveyed service providers expected MOFN services to generate revenue from connecting distributed AI compute clusters over the next three years.
CtrlS is deploying Ciena's WaveLogic 5 Extreme (WL5e)-powered Waveserver platform alongside the 6500 Reconfigurable Line System (RLS). The Waveserver platform is designed for high-capacity optical connectivity, while the 6500 RLS provides the optical transport infrastructure needed to scale network capacity. Ciena's broader technology roadmap reflects the direction of the optical industry. The company recently highlighted 1.6 Tb/s coherent optical capabilities and other technologies designed to support AI-scale networking. Although this CtrlS deployment uses WL5e, the broader evolution of Ciena's coherent optics portfolio illustrates the industry's move toward increasingly high-capacity optical transport.

Ciena reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $1.67 billion, up 37% year over year, and raised its fiscal 2026 revenue guidance to approximately $6.42 billion at the midpoint. Despite all the money pouring into the artificial intelligence boom, it feels like only a small handful of names have been consistent winners.
Plenty of companies quietly making that boom possible have been overlooked, their shares languishing while the giants soar. Ciena Corporation (NYSE: CIEN) is a good example.

Despite sitting right in the path of the AI wave, its stock has nonetheless tumbled more than 40% from its June high. However, that disconnect may be correcting itself.
After a punishing slide, the stock appears to have found a floor early this month and has started to turn higher, climbing around 17% in less than three weeks.

Even after its fall, Ciena is still up roughly 50% for the year, and the current bounce suggests investors are beginning to look again at a name they had written off. A well-timed vote of confidence from Wall Street this week has helped, making this a perfect time to ask if the market has been way too negative on Ciena's prospects.
That vote of confidence came from Evercore ISI, with analyst Amit Daryanani upgrading Ciena to Outperform earlier this week and setting a $550 price target. From where the stock trades today, that's around 50% upside, and just as importantly, Daryanani's argument cuts to the heart of the bull case: that Ciena sits at one of the AI boom's most overlooked bottlenecks.

This bottleneck theory is simple. Amid all the noise about chips and computing power, far less attention goes to how that data actually moves around. Modern AI systems shuttle staggering volumes of information between and within data centers, and doing so fast enough has become a serious constraint on how powerful they can be. Daryanani pinpointed connectivity as an increasingly critical bottleneck to the pace of AI's advancement.
This is Ciena's world. The company specializes in optical networking, the high-speed connections that carry data over long distances and, increasingly, across the sprawling AI facilities springing up everywhere. As one of the few dedicated names in the field, it's particularly well placed to benefit as those systems, and their data demands, keep growing.
The bullish case is more than a story, because the numbers behind it are seriously impressive. In its most recent quarterly report, released earlier this month, Ciena reported year-on-year revenue growth of 37% and earnings per share growth of 215%.
More telling still is the pipeline of future work. Ciena's management pointed to a swelling order book, with its backlog expected to top $10 billion by the end of its financial year, giving it, and the market, solid visibility into future revenue.
Ciena is also pushing into new territory. Beyond its traditional strength in long-distance links, it's developing products that operate inside data centers themselves, chasing a market it believes could be worth many billions. With leading technology and a clutch of new products, it has several ways to win rather than relying on a single one.
None of this means the risks have vanished. The stock's steep fall from its June high and the volatility that followed remind us how quickly sentiment can turn on a name like this. The biggest worry is simply that the AI spending spree may not last, and Ciena's fortunes are tightly bound to how much the cloud giants keep investing, so any slowdown would hit its orders hard.
There's also the matter of who its customers are. A handful of large clients account for a hefty slice of Ciena's revenue, with one customer alone making up close to 20%. Such concentration cuts both ways: it's fine while those customers spend freely, but it would hurt if even one pulled back.
Weighing it up, Ciena makes a compelling case as an underappreciated way to play the AI infrastructure boom. It sits at a real bottleneck, its core business is growing fast, its order book offers rare visibility, and Wall Street is clearly leaning toward the upside.
The caution comes not from the bulls but from the setup itself. Ciena's shares remain volatile, its valuation demands strong growth for years to come, and expectations will likely stay high after this week's upgrade. That tension, between an early-stage turnaround and a business with a lot still to prove, is what keeps the stock finely balanced.
For those who believe the AI buildout has years left to run, though, Ciena increasingly looks like one of its more overlooked beneficiaries, and this week's upgrade is a clear sign that others are already catching on.
